IR.rationale: Rising intermediate yields relative to the policy rate signal expected tightening. This hurts duration-heavy USD EM sovereign bonds and tightens funding for leveraged high-yield issuers.

B.rationale: Narrowing spreads together with strong HY returns describe easing credit conditions. Credit returns are positively autocorrelated because illiquidity and slow-moving capital make repricing gradual.

V.rationale: High equity implied volatility proxies a high price of risk. It is associated with larger subsequent risk premia in credit and EM spreads.

AP.rationale: Equity markets incorporate firm and country news before less liquid corporate and EM bond markets, a documented stock-to-bond lead-lag. Joint US and EM equity strength therefore signals broad risk-on repricing still to come in spreads.

ST.rationale: Weak momentum returns typically occur during junk-led rebounds after stress. These are states in which high-beta credit tends to keep recovering.

FX.rationale: Broad dollar strength combined with a weakening commodity and carry currency marks risk-off and tighter global dollar funding. This weighs on EM sovereign and high-yield credit.

COM.rationale: Energy issuers are a large share of the US HY index, and oil exporters weigh heavily in EM sovereign indices. Oil price gains therefore improve credit quality for both.

MC.rationale: Tight financial conditions reduce credit supply and raise default risk. They also raise the risk premium demanded, so they carry information about forward credit returns.

ENDG.rationale: HY and EM bond index returns show positive short-horizon autocorrelation from stale pricing and gradual flows.

IR.rationale: Abrupt repricing of the expected policy path triggers fund outflows and duration-driven turbulence in EM and HY bonds.

B.rationale: Widening spreads combined with HY losses mark a credit stress episode. In such episodes volatility clusters and liquidity deteriorates beyond what past realised variance captures.

V.rationale: Implied volatility is forward-looking. It contains information about future realised variance across risky assets beyond historical variance.

AP.rationale: Through the leverage and volatility-feedback mechanism, negative equity returns raise subsequent volatility in risky assets, including credit.

ST.rationale: Equity style factors carry little direct, robust information about credit volatility beyond the market and volatility groups.

FX.rationale: Yen appreciation together with Australian dollar weakness signals carry-trade unwinding and deleveraging. These episodes coincide with rising volatility in EM and HY assets.

COM.rationale: Oil price declines stress energy HY issuers and oil-exporting sovereigns, raising subsequent spread volatility.

MC.rationale: Elevated financial stress indexes capture funding and liquidity strains that forecast higher volatility in risky credit.

ENDG.rationale: Volatility is persistent. High recent variance relative to its own history may carry extra persistence in credit, where clustering is strong.

IR.rationale: Sharp rises in policy-sensitive yields can trigger outflows and large losses, especially in long-duration EM sovereign bonds.

B.rationale: An ongoing credit sell-off with widening spreads raises the chance of further large losses, through fire sales and the momentum of spread widening.

V.rationale: High implied volatility widens the return distribution and signals a risk-off regime, raising the probability of lower-tail outcomes.

AP.rationale: Joint US and EM equity weakness leads credit markets. It signals deteriorating fundamentals and risk appetite not yet fully priced in bonds.

ST.rationale: Style factor returns have no clear mechanism linking them to tail losses in credit.

FX.rationale: Dollar strength in a risk-off pattern tightens global dollar funding and hurts EM borrowers, raising tail risk for EM and HY bonds.

COM.rationale: Falling oil prices raise default risk among energy HY issuers and oil-exporting sovereigns, a key channel for large index losses.

MC.rationale: Elevated financial stress signals fragile liquidity and an elevated risk of disorderly credit sell-offs.

ENDG.rationale: Poor recent returns tend to be followed by further weakness in illiquid credit markets, because returns are autocorrelated and fund flows chase past performance.

IR.rationale: Falling yields relative to the policy rate, reflecting expected easing, support duration-sensitive EM bonds and ease funding for HY issuers.

B.rationale: Spread tightening with strong HY returns marks a recovery phase. Gradual capital return then tends to produce outsized subsequent gains.

V.rationale: High implied volatility both widens the distribution and raises risk premia. Large rebounds therefore most often follow high-volatility states.

AP.rationale: Strong US and EM equity returns lead credit. They signal a risk-on repricing that bonds tend to follow with a lag.

ST.rationale: Momentum underperformance accompanies junk rallies after stress, which are states with sharp rebounds in high-beta credit.

FX.rationale: Dollar weakness combined with commodity and carry currency strength signals easier global funding and risk appetite, favouring large gains in EM and HY bonds.

COM.rationale: Oil rebounds sharply improve the credit outlook of energy issuers and oil-exporting sovereigns.

MC.rationale: Large credit gains typically come as tight financial conditions start to ease and elevated risk premia are compressed. A tight-conditions state therefore helps identify that rebound potential.

ENDG.rationale: Positive return autocorrelation in illiquid credit makes strong recent performance informative for further large gains.
